vignette:
He is 35, a South Asian man who works as a tax consultant, and when he first talks about the year he spent as a relief worker in a war zone, he does so in the tidy, controlled way he uses to explain complicated tax rules to clients. He gives dates, locations, supply numbers. He lists what was distributed, how many families were processed, how the camp was organized. For a while, it sounds as if he is talking about logistics, not terror. Only gradually does the story become personal.

He had taken leave from his accounting firm in his late twenties, telling his wife he wanted to do something meaningful before settling fully into the routines of career and family. At first he feels useful there. He helps track shipments, organize records, and translate between aid staff and local families. He likes creating order in disorder. But the work quickly becomes something else. He sees children with burns and shrapnel wounds, parents clawing at supply trucks, old men sitting mute beside rubble where homes used to be. He learns to work while hearing artillery in the distance. Then one afternoon, while he is helping register displaced families outside a clinic, the shelling lands close. He remembers the sound first—an immense cracking roar that seems to split the air open—then dust, screaming, and the sensation that his body has become both unbearably heavy and unreal. When he gets up, his ears are ringing. A boy he had just spoken to is lying facedown near the wall. A nurse he knows is bleeding from the neck. He remembers trying to use his spreadsheet clipboard to press on a wound because there is nothing else in his hands.

After that day, the world does not return to normal. He continues working because everyone continues working. He tells himself that carrying boxes, checking lists, and escorting families to tents is the only decent thing to do. But he starts scanning every open space for cover. He jumps when metal doors slam. At night, in the crowded staff quarters, he lies awake waiting for the next impact, muscles braced so tightly that by morning his jaw aches. When he does sleep, he wakes drenched in sweat, sure for several seconds that the room is collapsing. He avoids the clinic courtyard where the shell hit, taking a longer route in the heat and pretending it is for efficiency. He also begins to feel ashamed. Others have lost children, limbs, homes; he is merely frightened. He does not tell anyone that sometimes, while entering supply figures, he suddenly sees the nurse’s blood on his hands again and has to leave the table before he vomits.

When he returns home, his family expects relief and gratitude. Instead he feels as if he has come back with his body but left some essential part of himself behind. His wife says he is quieter. He says he is tired and throws himself into work. Back at the tax firm, his colleagues praise his discipline; he is the one who catches small discrepancies, who stays late during filing season, who keeps immaculate records. The structure soothes him. Numbers behave predictably. Deadlines can be met. But even in the office he is never fully at ease. If someone drops a heavy binder or a truck backfires outside, his heart slams and he is on his feet before he knows why, embarrassed by the alarm on everyone else’s face. During meetings, when a client complains aggressively about penalties or audits, he feels a flash of disproportionate panic, as though the room has become dangerous. He hides it by becoming more formal, more precise.

At home, his wife notices the other changes he tries to minimize. He no longer sits with his back to a restaurant entrance. He checks news from conflict zones compulsively, then becomes irritable when she asks him to stop. He avoids weddings and crowded family gatherings because the noise, the crush of bodies, and the unpredictable bursts of laughter or fireworks leave him keyed up for hours. She has learned not to wake him suddenly. If she touches his shoulder while he is asleep, he comes up swinging or gasping, eyes wide and unrecognizing for a moment before shame floods in. He apologizes repeatedly, then withdraws for the rest of the morning.

He rarely speaks about the people he met there, but they are with him constantly. A child about the age of his nephew crying in a supermarket can make his chest tighten. The smell of antiseptic in a clinic waiting room makes his stomach turn. He keeps seeing the boy by the wall, not as a memory he chooses to revisit but as something that intrudes while he is brushing his teeth, reviewing a tax return, or trying to pray. He has begun to dread nighttime because sleep opens the door to scenes he cannot control. In the dreams he is always too slow, pinned in place, unable to carry enough supplies or stop the bleeding or warn anyone in time.

He tells himself he should be grateful. He has a stable job, a marriage, an apartment, parents who call every week. Yet he moves through much of his life as if danger is just out of sight. He is exhausted by the effort of appearing calm. What troubles him most is not only the fear but the distance it creates. His wife says he is physically present and emotionally elsewhere. He knows she is right. He wants to return to the version of himself who could laugh easily, plan for the future, and sit in a quiet room without listening for explosions that are no longer there.
